title: ⭐⭐ Revision: the order of an account, the beat of a line

questions.prompt: The listening passage of your module tells one family's story in four parts. Put these six moments of it back into the order in which they happened.

options.text: Natalie and Andy were married on the twenty-second of May.
The tsunami reached the stretch of coast where the couple were staying.
Natalie and Andy met at a swimming club.
The family set up a fund for the children the tsunami had orphaned.
The couple put the honeymoon off until Christmas, when Andy's design company would be quiet.
At the last minute they gave up New Zealand and booked a bungalow in Thailand.

questions.explanation: Every step carries the word that fixes it. The swimming club is placed about ten years before everything else and is the only moment that says how the two of them came to know each other, so nothing can stand in front of it. The wedding follows, in May. The honeymoon is put off after the wedding, and the reason given — the quiet season of Andy's design company — is what moves it to Christmas, so it comes third. The change of country is marked at the last minute, and a last minute only exists once a departure has been fixed, which is why it must follow the postponement and not precede it. The tsunami reaches a coast where the couple were already staying, so the booking has to be made before it. And the fund closes the account: it is the only step that looks back at the disaster instead of forward, and it is what the family did afterwards, for the children the same wave had orphaned.

questions.prompt: Your book gives be going to four uses, and one of them is commands and refusals — its own example being "You are going to take that medicine whether you like it or not". In which of these is be going to doing that?

options.text: He's going to buy a bicycle when the term ends.
It's going to be a dry summer, by the look of the fields.
The new library is going to stand at the edge of the town.
You're going to switch that tap off, like it or not.

questions.explanation: The sentence about the tap wears the clothes of a future and does not predict anything at all: the speaker is imposing, and like it or not is what gives him away, exactly as whether you like it or not does in your book's own example. The bicycle is a prior plan, the first of the four uses — somebody has decided and the term is the moment he acts. The dry summer read off the state of the fields is a prediction, the second use, and the evidence is standing in front of the speaker where anybody could point at it. And a library that is going to stand at the edge of the town describes a permanent state, the fourth use, which your book illustrates with a house that is going to look over the river.

questions.prompt: Two sentences about the same night. (1) "The family had to sleep in the school hall." (2) "The family must have slept in the school hall." What does the second one tell you that the first does not?

options.text: That the writer is concluding it, without having seen them.
That the writer knows they slept there and is telling you so.
That the writer thinks they ought to have slept there.
That the writer was obliged to let them sleep there.

questions.explanation: had to reports a fact: an obligation really applied, and the writer states it as he would state anything else he knows. must followed by have and a past participle reports a conclusion instead — the writer was not there, he works it out from something else, and must measures how sure he is rather than what obliged anybody. Saying that he knows and is telling you describes the first sentence, which is the one that claims nothing beyond the fact. Putting the obligation on the writer moves it to a person neither sentence mentions. And ought to have slept is what should have slept would say — a sensible thing that did not happen — which is a reproach, not a deduction.

questions.prompt: A pupil is writing her story of the storm. She wants to say that the roof went while she was on her way out with the last box: the carrying was already going on, and the roof went in an instant. Which sentence says that?

options.text: I carried the last box out when the roof went.
I was carrying the last box out when the roof went.
I carried the last box out while the roof was going.
I was carrying the last box out when the roof was going.

questions.explanation: Ask which of the two actions lasted. The carrying did, so it takes the past progressive and draws the background; the roof went in an instant, so it takes the simple past and drops inside that background: I was carrying the last box out when the roof went. Two simple pasts put the two events side by side on the same level, and the sentence then reads as though the roof went once the box was out. Putting the progressive on the roof instead makes the collapse the long action, which is exactly the wrong way round, and no roof goes slowly enough for that. And putting was going on the roof as well leaves nothing to interrupt anything: two long actions running side by side, when what the sentence needs is one long action cut across by an instant.

questions.prompt: Read this line aloud, as the pronunciation work of the module asks you to: "The water came through the door before we could reach it." English gives its beats to the words that carry the meaning. Which four words take them?

options.text: before, could, reach, we
the, through, the, before
water, came, door, reach
water, through, door, could

questions.explanation: The beat falls on the words that carry the meaning — nouns, main verbs, adjectives, adverbs — and this line has exactly four of them: water, came, door, reach. Everything else is there to hold the sentence together and is said quickly and quietly in between: the two articles, the preposition through, the conjunction before, the pronoun we, the pronoun it and the auxiliary could. That is why those little words are the hardest to catch when somebody speaks fast — the beats keep arriving at about the same rate, so whatever stands between two of them is compressed to fit. Any set that gives a beat to through or to could is picking a word that has no meaning of its own to carry, and the set made entirely of small words is the rhythm of the line turned inside out. The one thing that moves the beat is a contrast: say I meant the back door, not the front one, and back takes it.

questions.prompt: Read this note from a school project. "The hillside above the village had been cleared of its trees three years earlier. When the rain came, nothing held the soil, and the mud reached the first houses within an hour. The families had left the night before, because the mayor had read the forecast." Which of these states a cause and its own effect, as the note gives them?

options.text: The families left the village, so the mayor read the forecast.
The mud reached the houses, so the hillside was cleared of its trees.
The rain came, so the families had left the night before.
The trees had been cleared, so nothing held the soil.

questions.explanation: A cause comes before its effect, and the note is careful about the order. The hillside lost its trees three years earlier, and it is because nothing was left to hold the soil that the rain carried it away — cause, then effect, and the note joins them in that order. The second link the note gives is the forecast: the mayor read it, so the families left. That is what makes the sentence about the rain wrong, and wrong twice: the families had already gone the night before, so rain that came afterwards cannot be why they went, and the note's own because points at the forecast instead. Putting the mud before the clearing turns three years upside down. And the families cannot have caused the mayor to read anything, since the note says the reading came first.
